programme.title: Providers and Sensitive Data Follow Along
programme.outcome: Cover multiple providers, provider versioning, aliases, authentication methods and Terraform Associate 004 objective 4h, including sensitive values, state exposure, ephemeral/write-only patterns and Vault, using HCP Terraform global resources and AWS eu-west-2.
programme.region: HCP Terraform global/control-plane resources and AWS eu-west-2
programme.statusNotice: **Status:** Offline authoring manuscript only — not locally validated, imported, accepted, approved, published or fingerprinted.

examObjectivesCovered.text: Write Terraform configuration using multiple providers
Understand best practices for managing sensitive data, including secrets management with Vault
Initialize, validate, plan, apply and destroy during the provider exercises
Pass an aliased provider configuration into a child module
Inspect state to understand sensitive versus ephemeral persistence
Use HCP Terraform remote execution and integration with dynamic provider credentials

completionDefinition: A temporary AWS bootstrap IAM user and named CLI profile are created without root access keys.
Local AWS provider authentication through a shared profile is proven with a data-only configuration.
A dedicated HCP Terraform organization, project and CLI-driven remote workspace are created.
HCP Terraform authenticates the AWS provider with OIDC dynamic credentials rather than static AWS access keys.
The workspace has a default AWS credential configuration and a tagged LONDON credential configuration for an aliased provider.
The main configuration installs and versions AWS and Random providers and records selections in .terraform.lock.hcl.
The learner uses a default AWS provider, aws.london alias and explicit alias passing into a child module.
A stateful random_password and a fake sensitive Terraform variable demonstrate that redaction does not remove secrets from state.
An ephemeral random_password demonstrates a value that is not persisted in state.
A write-only resource argument pattern is reviewed without creating cost-bearing RDS infrastructure.
A local Vault development server and Terraform Vault provider read a fake secret, demonstrating both Vault usage and Terraform state implications.
All Terraform-managed AWS resources are destroyed before the HCP workspace/state, authentication resources, temporary credentials and local files are removed.

tasks.title: Verify accounts and local tools
tasks.goal: Confirm Terraform, AWS CLI, HCP Terraform access and a safe training AWS account before creating anything.
tasks.whyItMatters: Provider and authentication problems are much easier to diagnose when the CLI tools and account access are known to work first.
tasks.examRelevance: This Follow Along concentrates on 2a, 2b, 2c and 4h, while still using the normal init/plan/apply/destroy workflow.

browserSteps.instruction: Sign in to the AWS account that will be used only for training. Do not create resources yet.
Open https://app.terraform.io and confirm that you can sign in to HCP Terraform.
Open Windows PowerShell. Run the version checks below.
If Terraform is missing, install it from the official HashiCorp install page, then reopen PowerShell.
If AWS CLI is missing, install AWS CLI v2 from the official AWS guide, then reopen PowerShell.
Do not create or use root access keys. Root is used only for the one-time training IAM bootstrap in the next task.

cliBlocks.title: Tool checks
cliBlocks.content:
terraform version
aws --version

expectedResults: Terraform prints a version.
AWS CLI prints a version.
AWS and HCP Terraform browser sign-in both work.

verificationChecks.text: Both commands run without command-not-found errors.
No lab resource has been created yet.

tasks.title: Create the temporary IAM training identity
tasks.goal: Use root only to create a dedicated IAM user, console sign-in, access key and tightly-scoped training policy, then sign out of root.
tasks.whyItMatters: HCP Terraform will later use temporary role credentials, but the learner still needs a separate bootstrap identity to create the OIDC trust and verify resources.
tasks.examRelevance: Authentication is proving identity; authorization is deciding which API actions that identity can perform. The exam expects you to separate those concepts.
warnings: The bootstrap access key is temporary and must be removed during cleanup.

browserSteps.instruction: Sign in to AWS as the root user only for this bootstrap task.
Open IAM > Users > Create user.
Set the user name to fa-providers-terraform-admin. Enable AWS Management Console access so the rest of the browser route can be completed without root.
Create a customer managed policy named fa-providers-terraform-admin-policy using the JSON policy block supplied below, then attach it to fa-providers-terraform-admin.
Create one access key for fa-providers-terraform-admin for CLI training use. Copy the Access key ID and Secret access key immediately to a temporary secure place; AWS will not show the secret again.
Sign out of the root user.
Sign in as the new IAM user fa-providers-terraform-admin. Do not use root again until final deletion of this temporary training identity.
The access key is long-lived authentication. This lab uses it only for bootstrap/verification and deliberately does not store it in Terraform or HCP Terraform.

cliBlocks.title: No root CLI commands
cliBlocks.content:
# No root CLI command is required or permitted for this Follow Along.
# Complete this one-time bootstrap in the AWS IAM console.

expectedResults: The IAM user exists and can sign in to the AWS console.
Exactly one access key exists for the training user.
The custom policy is attached.
Root is signed out.

verificationChecks.text: IAM shows user fa-providers-terraform-admin.
Attached policies include fa-providers-terraform-admin-policy.
The browser session is the IAM user, not root.

tasks.title: Configure and verify the named AWS CLI profile
tasks.goal: Store the temporary IAM user's access key only in the named AWS CLI profile fa-providers-terraform-admin, verify the identity and derive deterministic HCP names.
tasks.whyItMatters: The named profile demonstrates shared-credentials-file authentication without hard-coding credentials in Terraform configuration.
tasks.examRelevance: AWS shared profiles are one provider authentication method; provider credentials should not be embedded directly in provider blocks.
warnings: Never paste the secret access key into Terraform .tf files or HCP workspace variables in this lab.

browserSteps.instruction: Open Windows PowerShell as your normal Windows user.
Run aws configure --profile fa-providers-terraform-admin. Paste the training user's Access key ID and Secret access key when prompted.
For Default region name enter eu-west-2. For output format enter json.
Run get-caller-identity and check that the ARN contains the training IAM user name.
Run the PowerShell variable commands below. They derive the HCP organization from your AWS account ID so you do not need to invent a placeholder name.
Record the printed values. They are used exactly in later browser steps and IAM trust.

cliBlocks.title: Create profile and derive lab names
cliBlocks.content:
aws configure --profile fa-providers-terraform-admin

$AWS_ACCOUNT_ID = aws sts get-caller-identity --profile fa-providers-terraform-admin --query Account --output text
$HCP_ORG = "fa-providers-terraform-$AWS_ACCOUNT_ID"
$HCP_PROJECT = "fa-providers-terraform-project"
$HCP_WORKSPACE = "fa-providers-terraform-providers-sensitive"

aws sts get-caller-identity --profile fa-providers-terraform-admin
"ACCOUNT_ID=$AWS_ACCOUNT_ID"
"HCP_ORG=$HCP_ORG"
"HCP_PROJECT=$HCP_PROJECT"
"HCP_WORKSPACE=$HCP_WORKSPACE"

expectedResults: get-caller-identity returns the correct AWS account.
The ARN identifies the training IAM user.
HCP_ORG is fa-providers-terraform followed by the 12-digit AWS account ID.

verificationChecks.text: AWS account ID is 12 digits.
The profile name is exactly fa-providers-terraform-admin.
HCP project/workspace names exactly match the printed values.

tasks.title: Prove local shared-profile provider authentication
tasks.goal: Use a small data-only local Terraform configuration to authenticate the AWS provider through the named CLI profile without creating AWS infrastructure.
tasks.whyItMatters: Seeing one successful local authentication path makes it easier to understand why HCP remote runners need a different authentication path later.
tasks.examRelevance: Objective 2b: providers authenticate to remote APIs; the authentication method is provider-specific. Static credentials in provider configuration are a bad practice.

browserSteps.instruction: Create a new folder C:\terraform-labs\fa-providers-terraform\auth-demo. If C:\terraform-labs does not exist, create it.
Inside auth-demo create a file named main.tf and paste the supplied Local AWS authentication demo configuration.
Notice that the provider block contains a profile name but no access key or secret key.
Run terraform init, terraform validate and terraform apply. This configuration uses only the aws_caller_identity data source, so it creates no AWS resource.
Compare the Terraform output account ID with aws sts get-caller-identity.

cliBlocks.title: Local shared-profile authentication
cliBlocks.content:
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force C:\terraform-labs\fa-providers-terraform\auth-demo | Out-Null
Set-Location C:\terraform-labs\fa-providers-terraform\auth-demo

terraform fmt
terraform init
terraform validate
terraform apply -auto-approve

aws sts get-caller-identity --profile fa-providers-terraform-admin --query Account --output text
terraform output authenticated_account_id

editableBlocks.title: auth-demo/main.tf

expectedResults: Terraform initializes the AWS provider.
terraform validate succeeds.
terraform apply reads the caller identity and reports no managed infrastructure creation.
The Terraform account ID matches the AWS CLI account ID.

verificationChecks.text: No access_key or secret_key argument exists in main.tf.
The two account IDs match.
AWS Resource Groups/SSM show no resource from this task.

tasks.title: Create the HCP Terraform organization, project and workspace
tasks.goal: Create dedicated HCP Terraform control-plane resources for the provider and sensitive-data exercises.
tasks.whyItMatters: A separate organization/project/workspace keeps the lab state and variables isolated and makes cleanup unambiguous.
tasks.examRelevance: HCP Terraform is not a provider; it supplies remote execution/state/collaboration while providers communicate with target APIs.
warnings: Treat the terraform login token as sensitive. Do not commit Terraform CLI credentials files.

browserSteps.instruction: In PowerShell rerun the three name derivation lines from Task 3 if the variables are no longer in your shell.
Open HCP Terraform in the browser.
Create an organization using the exact HCP_ORG value printed in Task 3. If HCP reports that the name is already taken, stop: do not reuse an unrelated organization for this lab.
Inside that organization create a project named fa-providers-terraform-project.
Inside the project create a CLI-driven workspace named fa-providers-terraform-providers-sensitive. Do not connect a VCS repository.
Open workspace Settings > General. Keep execution mode Remote. Select a stable Terraform version 1.11.0 or later; a current 1.15.x stable version is suitable.
Return to PowerShell and run terraform login. Follow the browser flow and paste the generated HCP Terraform token when prompted.
Do not print or copy the HCP CLI token into this manuscript or a .tf file.

cliBlocks.title: Rebuild names and authenticate Terraform CLI
cliBlocks.content:
$AWS_ACCOUNT_ID = aws sts get-caller-identity --profile fa-providers-terraform-admin --query Account --output text
$HCP_ORG = "fa-providers-terraform-$AWS_ACCOUNT_ID"
$HCP_PROJECT = "fa-providers-terraform-project"
$HCP_WORKSPACE = "fa-providers-terraform-providers-sensitive"

terraform login

expectedResults: The organization exists with the exact derived name.
The project contains the workspace.
The workspace uses Remote execution.
terraform login reports successful token retrieval/storage.

verificationChecks.text: HCP organization name ends with the current AWS account ID.
Project is fa-providers-terraform-project.
Workspace is fa-providers-terraform-providers-sensitive.
Workspace Terraform version is at least 1.11.0.

tasks.title: Create the HCP Terraform OIDC identity provider in AWS
tasks.goal: Create the AWS OIDC identity provider that allows AWS to validate HCP Terraform workload identity tokens.
tasks.whyItMatters: OIDC lets HCP Terraform exchange signed workload identity for short-lived AWS role credentials instead of storing AWS access keys in HCP.
tasks.examRelevance: Dynamic credentials are a best-practice provider authentication pattern because HCP receives temporary credentials only for the run.
warnings: If an app.terraform.io OIDC provider already exists from unrelated infrastructure, stop rather than deleting/replacing it.

browserSteps.instruction: In the AWS console, confirm you are signed in as the training IAM user, not root.
Open IAM > Identity providers > Add provider.
Choose OpenID Connect.
Provider URL: https://app.terraform.io
Audience: aws.workload.identity
Add the provider.
Open the new provider and verify the provider URL and audience exactly. Record its ARN.
Use either the Console route above OR the CLI create command below. Do not create the same OIDC provider twice.

cliBlocks.title: OIDC CLI alternative
cliBlocks.content:
# Run the create command only if you did NOT create the provider in the console.
aws iam create-open-id-connect-provider `
  --url https://app.terraform.io `
  --client-id-list aws.workload.identity `
  --profile fa-providers-terraform-admin

$AWS_ACCOUNT_ID = aws sts get-caller-identity --profile fa-providers-terraform-admin --query Account --output text
$OIDC_ARN = "arn:aws:iam::${AWS_ACCOUNT_ID}:oidc-provider/app.terraform.io"

aws iam get-open-id-connect-provider `
  --open-id-connect-provider-arn $OIDC_ARN `
  --profile fa-providers-terraform-admin

expectedResults: IAM contains one app.terraform.io OIDC identity provider for the lab.
The client ID/audience is aws.workload.identity.

verificationChecks.text: The OIDC provider ARN contains the current AWS account ID and app.terraform.io.
The audience exactly equals aws.workload.identity.

tasks.title: Create the restricted HCP Terraform AWS run role
tasks.goal: Create one role trusted only by this HCP organization/project/workspace and allow it to manage only /fa-providers-terraform/* SSM parameters.
tasks.whyItMatters: The trust policy limits who may assume the role, while the permissions policy limits what the assumed role may do.
tasks.examRelevance: Authentication (OIDC trust) and authorization (SSM permission policy) are separate. This distinction is central to understanding provider authentication securely.

browserSteps.instruction: In IAM open Roles > Create role.
Choose Web identity and select the app.terraform.io identity provider with audience aws.workload.identity.
Create a role named fa-providers-terraform-run-role.

Replace its trust policy with the exact trust structure shown below, substituting the AWS account ID and HCP organization value you derived in Task 3. The subject must remain restricted to this project, workspace and run_phase:*.

Create an inline permissions policy named fa-providers-terraform-run-policy using the supplied JSON. It can manage only SSM parameters under /fa-providers-terraform/* in eu-west-2 plus DescribeParameters.
Do not attach AdministratorAccess.
Record the role ARN.

cliBlocks.title: Create the HCP run role and inline policy

expectedResults: The role exists.
The trust policy checks app.terraform.io:aud and a workspace-specific app.terraform.io:sub.
The inline policy manages only the training SSM parameter path.

verificationChecks.text: Role name is exactly fa-providers-terraform-run-role.
Trust subject contains the exact organization/project/workspace.
No AdministratorAccess policy is attached.

tasks.title: Configure default and aliased AWS dynamic credentials plus a sensitive variable
tasks.goal: Configure HCP Terraform to generate two AWS dynamic credential configurations and store one fake sensitive Terraform input.
tasks.whyItMatters: This demonstrates alias-specific authentication without duplicating long-lived access keys and shows that HCP variable sensitivity is a display/access control, not a guarantee that Terraform state cannot contain the value.
tasks.examRelevance: Multiple dynamic credential configurations use tagged environment variables. Sensitive workspace variables hide values after entry, but downstream Terraform usage can still persist values in state.
warnings: Use only the literal fake value training-secret-not-real. Never substitute a real password, API token or production secret.

browserSteps.instruction: Open HCP Terraform > fa-providers-terraform-providers-sensitive > Variables.
Add Environment variable TFC_AWS_PROVIDER_AUTH with value true. Leave Sensitive off.
Add Environment variable TFC_AWS_PROVIDER_AUTH_LONDON with value true. Leave Sensitive off. LONDON is the tag for the aliased provider credential configuration.
Add Environment variable TFC_DEFAULT_AWS_RUN_ROLE_ARN with the ARN of fa-providers-terraform-run-role. Leave Sensitive off; an IAM role ARN is not a secret.
Add Environment variable TF_VAR_training_secret with value training-secret-not-real and turn Sensitive ON before saving.
Add Terraform variable aws_region with value eu-west-2, or rely on the default in variables.tf. Do not create AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID or AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY variables in HCP Terraform.
After saving TF_VAR_training_secret, confirm HCP no longer displays its value.
Understand the design: the default and LONDON configurations each request their own workload identity token, while the default role ARN supplies the same lab role to both.

cliBlocks.title: No secret CLI export
cliBlocks.content:
# Configure these values in the HCP Terraform workspace Variables page.
# Do not export the fake training secret into your general shell profile.

expectedResults: HCP Variables contains TFC_AWS_PROVIDER_AUTH=true.
HCP Variables contains TFC_AWS_PROVIDER_AUTH_LONDON=true.
TFC_DEFAULT_AWS_RUN_ROLE_ARN points to the lab run role.
TF_VAR_training_secret is marked Sensitive.
No static AWS access key is stored in HCP.

verificationChecks.text: Both provider-auth toggles exist.
The role ARN is correct.
The fake training secret is masked in the HCP UI.
There is no AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY variable in the workspace.

tasks.title: Build the multi-provider Terraform configuration
tasks.goal: Create the complete HCP Terraform configuration with AWS, an AWS alias, Random, a child module and sensitive/ephemeral demonstrations.
tasks.whyItMatters: This is the main practical exercise for objectives 2a, 2b, 2c and 4h.
tasks.examRelevance: 2a: install/version providers. 2b: provider blocks configure API clients. 2c: multiple providers and aliases. 4h: sensitive/ephemeral handling.

browserSteps.instruction: Create C:\terraform-labs\fa-providers-terraform\hcp-main and a child folder modules\alias-demo.
Create versions.tf, variables.tf, providers.tf, main.tf, outputs.tf, .gitignore, modules\alias-demo\versions.tf and modules\alias-demo\main.tf.
Paste the supplied blocks into the matching files exactly.
Notice required_providers declares two provider TYPES: hashicorp/aws and hashicorp/random.

Notice there are two CONFIGURATIONS of the AWS provider: the default and aws.london. Both target eu-west-2 so this lab remains in the requested Region; the alias demonstrates configuration selection rather than cross-Region deployment.
Notice HCP Terraform supplies the tfc_aws_dynamic_credentials object at run time. The default provider uses .default.shared_config_file and aws.london uses aliases["LONDON"].shared_config_file.
Notice the child module declares configuration_aliases = [aws.london], and the root module passes aws.london explicitly.
Notice random_password.persisted_demo is a normal managed logical resource, while ephemeral.random_password.ephemeral_demo is intentionally not persisted in state.
Notice .gitignore excludes local state and tfvars but DOES NOT exclude .terraform.lock.hcl; the lock file should normally be committed to version control.

cliBlocks.title: Create directories
cliBlocks.content:
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force C:\terraform-labs\fa-providers-terraform\hcp-main\modules\alias-demo | Out-Null
Set-Location C:\terraform-labs\fa-providers-terraform\hcp-main

editableBlocks.title: hcp-main/versions.tf
hcp-main/variables.tf
hcp-main/providers.tf
hcp-main/main.tf
hcp-main/outputs.tf
hcp-main/modules/alias-demo/versions.tf
hcp-main/modules/alias-demo/main.tf

expectedResults: All eight files exist.
No AWS access key, secret key, Vault token or HCP token appears in any .tf file.
The configuration has AWS and Random required providers plus the aws.london alias.

verificationChecks.text: versions.tf contains cloud {} and both provider requirements.
providers.tf contains default aws, aws.london and random provider blocks.
Child module declares configuration_aliases.
training_secret is marked sensitive.
The ephemeral random_password block exists.

tasks.title: Initialize providers and inspect the dependency lock file
tasks.goal: Connect the directory to the existing HCP workspace, install provider plugins and inspect the exact selected versions recorded in .terraform.lock.hcl.
tasks.whyItMatters: The exam distinguishes the version constraints you write from the concrete provider selections Terraform records in the dependency lock file.
tasks.examRelevance: Objective 2a explicitly covers installing/versioning providers and the dependency lock file.

browserSteps.instruction: Open PowerShell in hcp-main.
Rebuild HCP_ORG from the AWS account ID if needed.
Set TF_CLOUD_ORGANIZATION and TF_WORKSPACE only for this PowerShell session. The empty cloud {} block reads these values.
Run terraform fmt -recursive, terraform init and terraform validate.
Run terraform providers and inspect how the root and child module require providers.
Open .terraform.lock.hcl. Find hashicorp/aws and hashicorp/random and note the concrete versions Terraform selected.
Run terraform init -upgrade once. With the current constraints, Terraform checks for the newest acceptable provider versions and updates the lock selection only if needed.
Do not manually edit .terraform.lock.hcl.

cliBlocks.title: Initialize and inspect providers
cliBlocks.content:
Set-Location C:\terraform-labs\fa-providers-terraform\hcp-main

$AWS_ACCOUNT_ID = aws sts get-caller-identity --profile fa-providers-terraform-admin --query Account --output text
$env:TF_CLOUD_ORGANIZATION = "fa-providers-terraform-$AWS_ACCOUNT_ID"
$env:TF_WORKSPACE = "fa-providers-terraform-providers-sensitive"

terraform fmt -recursive
terraform init
terraform validate
terraform providers
Get-Content .terraform.lock.hcl
terraform init -upgrade
terraform validate

expectedResults: terraform init says HCP Terraform initialized successfully.
AWS and Random provider plugins install or reuse locked versions.
terraform validate succeeds.
terraform providers shows root requirements and the child module AWS requirement.
.terraform.lock.hcl exists.

verificationChecks.text: .terraform.lock.hcl contains registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws.
.terraform.lock.hcl contains registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/random.
The child module is visible in terraform providers output.
Validation reports Success.

tasks.title: Run the remote plan and apply with multiple provider configurations
tasks.goal: Use HCP Terraform remote execution to authenticate both AWS configurations dynamically and create only the small training resources.
tasks.whyItMatters: A successful apply proves that provider installation, default/aliased authentication, module provider passing and sensitive input handling all work together.
tasks.examRelevance: Provider aliases select specific configurations; dynamic credentials authenticate each configuration; sensitive outputs redact normal display.
warnings: The fake training_secret is intentionally allowed into state for the next objective-4h demonstration. Never perform that step with a real secret.

browserSteps.instruction: In PowerShell run terraform plan. The local CLI uploads the configuration and HCP Terraform performs the remote operation.
Open the run link shown by Terraform or open the workspace Runs page in your browser.

Review the plan before applying. Expected managed additions are four SSM parameters plus one normal random_password logical resource. The ephemeral random_password is not a persisted managed resource.
Confirm every AWS SSM name begins /fa-providers-terraform/.
Run terraform apply and type yes only after the plan is correct.
Watch the HCP run until it finishes Applied.
Do not copy sensitive output values from HCP or state.

cliBlocks.title: Remote plan and apply
cliBlocks.content:
Set-Location C:\terraform-labs\fa-providers-terraform\hcp-main
terraform plan
terraform apply

expectedResults: The remote plan succeeds without AWS access-key variables.
The plan contains /fa-providers-terraform/default-provider, /aliased-provider, /sensitive-demo and /module-alias.
Apply finishes successfully.
Outputs for persisted_password_demo and training_secret_echo are shown as sensitive/redacted.

tasks.title: Compare sensitive redaction with actual state storage
tasks.goal: Show that sensitive=true hides values from normal output but does not automatically remove them from Terraform state.
tasks.whyItMatters: This is one of the most important objective-4h distinctions: redaction protects accidental display; state access still requires strong security controls.
tasks.examRelevance: Objective 4h: sensitive does not mean 'not stored'. Ephemeral values and provider write-only arguments are the tools designed to avoid persistence when supported.
warnings: The raw state command can expose secrets. Use only the fake lab value and never paste state output into external systems.

browserSteps.instruction: Run terraform output. Confirm persisted_password_demo and training_secret_echo display as sensitive rather than showing their values.
Run terraform state list. Confirm random_password.persisted_demo is listed.

Do not run state-pull searches for real secrets in shared terminals, tickets or screen recordings.
Open HCP Terraform > workspace > States and note that HCP retains state versions. State access itself must be protected.

tasks.whyItMatters: Good secret handling includes removing unnecessary secret consumers, but historical state versions may still contain older values and must remain protected.

tasks.title: Review provider, authentication and objective 4h exam points
tasks.goal: Turn the completed hands-on work into a clear Terraform Associate 004 mental model before cleanup.
tasks.whyItMatters: The exam tests concepts rather than AWS-specific memorization, so the learner should be able to describe the general Terraform behavior shown by the lab.
tasks.examRelevance: Official exam mapping: 2a provider installation/versioning, 2b provider use, 2c multiple providers, 4h sensitive data including Vault.

browserSteps.instruction: Provider requirement: required_providers tells Terraform the provider source and acceptable versions.
Provider installation: terraform init installs/selects providers and writes concrete selections/checksums to .terraform.lock.hcl.
Provider block: configures a provider client, such as region or authentication-related settings.
Multiple provider types: this lab used AWS, Random and Vault.
Provider aliases: aws.london is a second configuration of the AWS provider. A resource/module must explicitly select/receive it; declaring an alias alone changes nothing.
Modules: provider configurations are defined in the root; child modules declare requirements and configuration_aliases, then the root can pass providers explicitly.

Authentication: local shared profile used long-lived bootstrap credentials; HCP remote runs used OIDC dynamic short-lived role credentials; Vault provider used a token from an environment variable instead of hard-coding it.
Sensitive: sensitive=true redacts normal display but values can still exist in state.
Ephemeral: values/resources marked/defined as ephemeral are omitted from persistent plan/state artifacts and may be used only in allowed ephemeral contexts.
Write-only: provider-defined write-only resource arguments accept values during an operation without persisting those argument values.
Vault: centralizes secrets and can issue dynamic secrets/credentials, but Terraform configurations using Vault must still protect state and avoid unnecessary secret persistence.

troubleshooting.title: terraform init cannot select the HCP organization or workspace
troubleshooting.likelyCause: TF_CLOUD_ORGANIZATION or TF_WORKSPACE is not set in the current shell, or terraform login has not completed.
troubleshooting.fix: Rebuild HCP_ORG from the AWS account ID, set both environment variables, run terraform login if needed, then rerun terraform init.

troubleshooting.title: HCP plan fails with no valid credential sources
troubleshooting.likelyCause: One or more TFC_AWS_* dynamic credential variables are missing, or static AWS arguments interfere with HCP dynamic credentials.
troubleshooting.fix: Confirm TFC_AWS_PROVIDER_AUTH=true, TFC_AWS_PROVIDER_AUTH_LONDON=true and TFC_DEFAULT_AWS_RUN_ROLE_ARN is correct; remove access_key/secret_key/profile arguments from the HCP AWS provider blocks.

troubleshooting.title: Invalid index for tfc_aws_dynamic_credentials.aliases["LONDON"]
troubleshooting.likelyCause: The LONDON tagged dynamic credential configuration was not created in HCP Terraform.
troubleshooting.fix: Add Environment variable TFC_AWS_PROVIDER_AUTH_LONDON=true, keep the default run role ARN, save, and queue a new run.

troubleshooting.title: AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity AccessDenied
troubleshooting.likelyCause: The role trust subject does not exactly match organization, project, workspace or run phase, or the audience is wrong.
troubleshooting.fix: Compare the trust policy with the exact recorded HCP names and aws.workload.identity audience. Do not broaden the trust to all organizations.

troubleshooting.title: AccessDenied on ssm:PutParameter
troubleshooting.likelyCause: The run role inline policy is missing an action or the parameter name is outside /fa-providers-terraform/*.
troubleshooting.fix: Keep the parameter names under the exact training prefix and compare the inline policy with the supplied policy; do not grant AdministratorAccess.

troubleshooting.title: Child module reports missing provider configuration aws.london
troubleshooting.likelyCause: configuration_aliases or the root module providers map is missing.
troubleshooting.fix: Ensure child versions.tf declares configuration_aliases=[aws.london] and the root module block maps aws.london = aws.london.

troubleshooting.title: terraform output says a sensitive value cannot be displayed
troubleshooting.likelyCause: The output is marked sensitive as intended.
troubleshooting.fix: Do not remove sensitive=true merely to reveal it. This lab uses state pull only with an explicitly fake value to demonstrate persistence.

troubleshooting.title: Fake training secret remains in current state after Task 14
troubleshooting.likelyCause: A resource/output still references var.training_secret or the apply was not completed.
troubleshooting.fix: Search the .tf files for training_secret, keep only the variable declaration, apply the removals, then pull current state again.

troubleshooting.title: vault status returns connection refused
troubleshooting.likelyCause: The local Vault dev server stopped or VAULT_ADDR is missing.
troubleshooting.fix: Restart the dev server in terminal A and set VAULT_ADDR=http://127.0.0.1:8200 in terminal B.

troubleshooting.title: Vault provider returns permission denied
troubleshooting.likelyCause: VAULT_TOKEN is absent/wrong in the terminal running Terraform.
troubleshooting.fix: For this dev-only exercise set VAULT_TOKEN=fa-providers-terraform-dev-token in that terminal. Never put the token in main.tf.

troubleshooting.title: Destroy plan contains an unexpected AWS resource
troubleshooting.likelyCause: Wrong HCP workspace/environment variables or an unintended resource was added.
troubleshooting.fix: Cancel destroy immediately. Verify TF_CLOUD_ORGANIZATION, TF_WORKSPACE and terraform state list before retrying.

troubleshooting.title: IAM refuses to create a second app.terraform.io OIDC provider
troubleshooting.likelyCause: That issuer already exists in the AWS account.
troubleshooting.fix: Do not overwrite or delete an existing shared provider. Stop and determine ownership before continuing; this manuscript assumes no pre-existing infrastructure.
